extracted.intended_audience: general readers; aspiring writers, conversationalists, and young tradesmen/apprentices
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, first-person guidance on improving one's mind, study habits, rhetorical manner, writing tactics, and personal conduct as an apprentice/tradesman, drawn from autobiographical examples. Emphasizes temperance, self-study, modest expression, and prudent industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance in eating and drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance in eating and drinking produces 'greater clearness of head and quicker apprehension'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and mental progress are aided by moderate diet; the author notes that, when living frugally (often only a biscuit, a handful of raisins, a tart, and a glass of water), he made greater progress because of the clearer head and quicker apprehension that attend temperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-directed study of foundational books
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn by independent reading of core textbooks and essays (e.g., Cocker's Arithmetick, Seller's and Shermy's Navigation, geometry, Locke's On Human Understanding, Art of Thinking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ashamed of ignorance, take a foundational text and work through it yourself; use accessible practical manuals (arithmetick, navigation) and philosophical works to sharpen reasoning. The author reports moving through these works alone with ease and gaining practical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the Socratic (humble-inquirer) method carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Socratic method — 'put on the humble inquirer and doubter' — to draw concessions and expose contradictions in interlocutors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method can be very effective for persuading or exposing inconsistency: the author practiced it to entangle even superior knowledge into concessions. Caveat: it can be embarrassing to others and ethically tricky (the author eventually left it, retaining only modest expression). It's especially useful if one genuinely has doubts or seeks information; overuse can be manipulative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express opinions with modest diffidence (avoid dogmatism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using positive, assuming words such as 'certainly' or 'undoubtedly'; instead say 'I conceive', 'it appears to me', 'I should think', 'I imagine', or 'if I am not mistaken'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modest phrasing ('I conceive', 'it appears to me') helps to inform, obtain information, please, and persuade; a positive, dogmatical manner 'seldom fails to disgust, tends to create opposition, and to defeat' conversational aims. Specific anti-pattern: using words that give the air of positiveness provokes contradiction and prevents candid attention from modest, sensible listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach and propose ideas with seeming diffidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Present unknown things as 'things forgot' and 'speak, tho' sure, with seeming diffidence' (citing Pope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When instructing or proposing ideas, framing them gently increases receptivity. The author endorses teaching as if you taught not, and proposing things unknown as things forgotten — i.e., adopt a humble tone to encourage attention and reduce antagonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anonymous publication to test reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit writing anonymously (e.g., slip an unsigned paper under the press door) to gauge impartial reception and criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author placed anonymous pieces in his brother's printing-house and learned from unbiased reaction of readers and commentators; this can be a deliberate tactic to learn how work is judged without authorial bias. Example: several anonymous pieces were approv'd and commented on by discerning acquaintances, which encouraged him to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix narration and dialogue to engage readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining narration and dialogue (as in Bunyan, Defoe, Richardson) makes writing more engaging, bringing the reader 'into the company and present at the discourse'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narration interspersed with dialogue increases reader engagement at the most interesting parts; the author cites Pilgrim's Progress and Defoe's works as models and notes Richardson's use of the technique in Pamela.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lampooning and libelling if you seek esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not indulge in lampooning or libelling; they harm reputation and standing in the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's father advised avoiding lampooning and libelling so as to obtain general esteem; the author himself was warned that indiscreet disputations about religion made him be pointed at as an infidel or atheist. Anti-pattern: writing that provokes authorities (e.g., a newspaper piece that offended the Assembly) can lead to censorship and personal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steady industry and prudent parsimony for business success
rubrics_metrics.description: By steady industry and a prudent parsimony one may save enough to set up in business; combine hard work with thrift to accumulate capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical vocational advice: work diligently, live frugally, and save toward establishing an independent business. The author's father counseled this as the proper route for a young tradesman rather than relying on premature patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unfair advantage and dishonorable shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not take unfair or deceitful advantage (e.g., using a forged or secret indenture) to escape obligations; such acts can be reckoned among one's 'errata'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reflects that assuming the name on the press and using a contrivance to avoid apprenticeship obligations was 'one of the first errata of my life' — a cautionary note that unfair maneuvers, even if expedient, are ethically suspect and can weigh on one's character/reputation.
